idiom_name: Node interface with a Children() []Node method
implementation_notes: Go replaces the abstract base class with an interface: type Node interface { Children() []Node }, implemented by every concrete struct that carries its node-specific fields, so generic passes are ordinary functions over Node and per-node dispatch is a type switch. The standard library is the reference realization - go/ast declares heterogeneous concrete node types under the ast.Node interface and walks any of them uniformly with ast.Inspect - so for a Go toolchain the normalized shape is the default, not a workaround. A base struct can hold shared position data by embedding, but children must go through the interface method.
pitfalls: Children() returning []Node allocates on every call; cache the slice in the node or provide a VisitChildren(func(Node) bool) iterator (the go/ast approach) when traversals are hot.
An interface value holding a typed nil pointer is not nil: a missing child stored as (*Binary)(nil) still satisfies Node and panics on first use - check for nil children explicitly.
The returned slice aliases the node's internal state if the node stores children directly; callers can mutate the tree by writing into it.
